title: "The uniform distribution"

Some linguistic measurements are bounded even when their observed distributions are not flat. The **uniform distribution** separates these two ideas: its support may be appropriate while its equal-density assumption may fail. Its [cumulative distribution function](cumulative-distribution-functions.qmd) will let us compare threshold probabilities under the flat reference with the observed Provo values.

We define the Provo predictability measurement, fit the uniform density on its admissible interval, and then compare that flat reference with the observed concentration of values.

## Provo modeled predictability

Luke and Christianson ([2018](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0908-4)) collected cloze norms and eye movements for English passages in the [Provo Corpus](https://osf.io/sjefs/). The table used here contains complete content word positions from the source passages. Each row aggregates the contributing reader trials for one word position; individual participant trials are therefore no longer the analysis rows.

Our variable, `OrthoMatchModel`, is the source authors' fitted
orthographic-cloze value from a logit mixed model with a random intercept by
word. The model combines the norming responses through its fitted fixed and
random effects, so the resulting value is model-derived. A raw cloze proportion
would instead divide the exact target matches at that position by the number of
norming responses. The prepared table does not retain those individual norming
responses, and the analysis below does not propagate uncertainty from the
first-stage fit.

The raw cloze task asks norming participants to continue a passage fragment;
orthographic match records whether a response matches the target word's
spelling. `OrthoMatchModel` is the source model's position-level prediction of
that match probability. The eye-tracking release also contains first fixation
duration, the time from the eyes' first landing on a word until they leave that
initial fixation. The preparation filters to positive durations, takes the
log duration within each retained reader trial, and stores the mean log
first fixation duration among positive fixations as `mean_log_ffd`;
`n_fixations` records how many positive-fixation trials contributed.

The first verified row is position 2 of passage 1, a three-character verb at
sentence position 2, with `OrthoMatchModel = 0.390221218`, mean log
first fixation duration `5.167650878`, and 60 contributing fixations. The
prepared table omits passage text and word strings, so a source
sentence cannot be reproduced from the available table. Position rather than reader
trial is the unit on this page, and `position_id` combines passage and word
number.

```{r}
#| label: load-provo-uniform
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
x <- provo$OrthoMatchModel
quartiles <- unname(quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.75)))

uniform_density <- data.frame(
  probability = c(0, 1),
  density = dunif(c(0, 1), min = 0, max = 1)
)
reference_probability <- punif(quartiles[2]) - punif(quartiles[1])

stopifnot(
  nrow(provo) == 1593L,
  length(unique(provo$Text_ID)) == 55L,
  all(x > 0 & x < 1),
  abs(reference_probability - diff(quartiles)) < 1e-12
)

data.frame(
  n_positions = length(x),
  empirical_mean = mean(x),
  empirical_variance = var(x),
  first_quartile = quartiles[1],
  third_quartile = quartiles[2],
  uniform_interval_probability = reference_probability
)
```

## Definition

For $X\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(a,b)$,

$$
f_X(x)
=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{b-a},&a\leq x\leq b,\\[4pt]
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

Integrating the density gives

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{a+b}{2},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[X]=\frac{(b-a)^2}{12},
$$

and for $a\leq c<d\leq b$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(c\leq X\leq d)=\frac{d-c}{b-a}.
$$

The CDF is

$$
F_X(x)
=\begin{cases}
0,&x<a,\\
\dfrac{x-a}{b-a},&a\leq x\leq b,\\
1,&x>b.
\end{cases}
$$

Integrating the first two raw moments gives

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]
=\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b x\,\mathrm dx
=\frac{a+b}{2},
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2
=\frac{(b-a)^2}{12}.
$$

Because this is a continuous distribution, $\mathbb{P}(X=x)=0$ for every exact point $x$, even where the density is positive. <!-- dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation -->

Using the source-defined unit interval and the empirical quartiles as $c$ and $d$, the uniform reference assigns probability `r sprintf("%.3f", reference_probability)` to that interval. The endpoints were not selected to create a convenient result.

Why use a uniform distribution at all? Its unit-interval support matches a
probability-valued prediction, and its flat density provides a simple baseline:
equal-width subintervals receive equal probability. It is not a plausible
model of cloze responses, reader trials, or the first-stage fitted values. The
comparison asks which feature fails after support has been matched.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-uniform
#| fig-cap: "Observed distribution of Provo modeled predictability with a unit-interval uniform reference."
ggplot(data.frame(probability = x), aes(probability)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 24,
                 fill = "grey75", color = "white") +
  geom_line(data = uniform_density, aes(probability, density),
            color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.85, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Modeled orthographic predictability", y = "Density") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The support is correct, but the histogram is concentrated near zero. A bounded response thus does not imply a uniform distribution.

## Check your understanding

1. Compare the empirical mean with the unit-interval uniform mean.
2. Compute the uniform reference probability between the empirical minimum and median.
3. Why does the histogram not represent participant-level ratings?
4. Which part of the uniform model fails here: support or density shape?
5. Why can the 1,593 rows not be treated as 1,593 [independent](../foundations/independence.qmd) readers? <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The empirical mean modeled predictability is 0.146337, far below the unit-uniform mean $\mathbb{E}[X]=0.5$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The empirical minimum is 0.004972 and the median is 0.026630, so the unit-uniform reference assigns their interval probability $0.026630-0.004972=0.021658$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Each row is a Provo word position carrying the source model's aggregated
   predictability estimate. Individual participant cloze ratings were inputs
   to that first-stage model and are absent from this table. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The unit-interval support is appropriate because every value lies strictly between zero and one, but the flat density shape fails to match the concentration near zero. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. A row aggregates a word position across contributing reader trials, and
   positions also share passages. Neither row count nor `n_fixations` counts
   independent readers.

</details>

`OrthoMatchModel` is a first-stage prediction at a word position. A uniform
model matches its support but imposes a flat density, an assumption rejected by
the empirical shape. The [beta distribution](beta-distribution.qmd) retains
the bounded support while estimating that shape.
